user_query: What explains node2vec's strong scalability on Barabási-Albert graphs with increasing average degree, and why does it still generate one million node representations so quickly?
llm_response: node2vec scales well on Barabási–Albert graphs because its training cost is driven mainly by the number of random-walk transitions and the cost of sampling neighbors, and the implementation uses efficient preprocessing plus alias-table sampling so each step is close to O(1). As the average degree increases, the graph becomes denser, but node2vec’s biased second-order walks still avoid expensive full-neighborhood computations and can reuse precomputed transition probabilities, so the runtime grows much more slowly than a naive method would. It can still generate one million node representations quickly because the algorithm is highly parallelizable, uses stochastic mini-batch training with negative sampling, and only needs to learn embeddings from sampled walk contexts rather than from all node pairs; in practice, the bottleneck is usually the walk generation and lightweight SGD updates, both of which are efficient enough to handle million-node graphs fast.
llm_confidence_reasoning: This explanation matches the standard node2vec algorithmic design and its known efficiency characteristics, though exact runtime behavior depends on implementation details and hardware.
